summary: The second part of Privacy Enhanced Mail. It covers certificate based key management, meaning how keys are issued and trusted. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1422.

plainLanguage.summary: To lock mail you need keys, and people need to trust they are the right ones. This explains how keys are handed out and checked.

questions: how do you validate a certificate
subtitle: How to issue and trust encryption keys for secure email

tldr.problem: Privacy Enhanced Mail needs a way to distribute and verify the public keys that protect messages. Users must be able to trust that a key actually belongs to the person they are emailing.
tldr.mechanism: Certification authorities (organizations like RSADSI) sign digital certificates that bind a person's identity to their public key. A hierarchical chain of certificates allows any recipient to validate that a key is genuine by checking signatures up to a trusted root authority.
tldr.outcome: This framework enabled secure email in the early Internet, though it was replaced by RFC 1422, which superseded this approach.

today: RFC 1114 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 1422, which refined the certificate-based key management approach for Privacy Enhanced Mail.

sections.title: Introduction to PEM Key Management
sections.content:
RFC 1114 is the second part of Privacy Enhanced Mail. RFC 1113 describes how to encrypt and sign messages; this RFC describes how to distribute and validate the public keys that make encryption possible.

The core problem is trust. When you receive an encrypted message, you need the recipient's public key to decrypt a message sent to you, or you need to send your own public key to someone who wants to email you securely. But how do you know the key you receive actually belongs to that person and not an impostor?

PEM solves this by using digital certificates. A trusted organization (called a certification authority) signs a statement saying, "I have verified that this key belongs to this person." The signature on that certificate can be checked using the authority's own public key, creating a chain of trust.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to mail someone a locked box, they need your key to open it. But how do they know it is really your key? A trusted referee (a certification authority) can write a signed note: "Yes, this is really Alice's key." Your friend can check the referee's signature, and then trust your key.

sections.title: The Certificate Hierarchy
sections.content:
PEM organizes certificates in a simple two-level hierarchy. At the top is RSADSI (RSA Data Security, Inc.), which certifies the public keys of organizations. At the bottom are users, whose certificates are issued by their organization.

Each organization designates an Organizational Notary (ON) who verifies users' identities and submits their certificate requests to RSADSI. This separation of duties means RSADSI never holds users' secrets and organizations are responsible for knowing who they employ.

RSADSI itself holds the organization's private key, used only to sign certificates (not to decrypt messages). This centralizes the security burden: RSADSI protects the key with strict physical and procedural safeguards, and organizations do not have to.
sections.plainLanguage: The referee (RSADSI) certifies the company managers. Each company manager certifies their employees. That way the referee does not have to know every employee, and each company vouches for its own people.

sections.title: What a Certificate Contains
sections.content:
A certificate is a signed document containing seven parts. It identifies the subject (the person or organization the certificate is for), the issuer (who signed it), the validity period (the start and end dates it is valid), the public key, and a signature that proves the issuer really signed it.

The public key component is an RSA modulus between 320 and 632 bits long. Each certificate has a unique serial number within its issuer's namespace, used to identify it in revocation lists.

Certificates are designed to be transmitted openly (even in unencrypted email) because they contain only public information. A recipient needs only to check the signature against the issuer's public key to verify the certificate has not been forged.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate is a card that says: "This is Alice. Her public key is 12345. It is valid until next year. Signed by her company." Anyone can see it, but only the company can have written it.

sections.title: Validating Certificates
sections.content:
To validate a certificate, a recipient first checks the signature on it using the issuer's public key. If the signature is valid, the certificate has not been forged. Then the recipient checks the Distinguished Name (the identity fields in the certificate) to confirm it belongs to the intended person.

The hierarchy allows this to be done in just two steps: check the user certificate against the organization's public key (obtained from the organization's certificate), then check the organization certificate against RSADSI's public key (which RSADSI distributes out-of-band). If both signatures match, the user certificate is trusted.

To prevent mistakes, a user registration process includes a message hash sent both electronically and on paper. A user computes the hash over their identifying information and public key, then verifies the hashes match when they receive their certificate, confirming nothing was altered.
sections.plainLanguage: Check Alice's certificate against her company's key. If it matches, the company really signed it. Then check the company's certificate against the referee's key. If that matches too, you can trust Alice's key.

sections.title: Certificate Revocation and Lifecycle
sections.content:
A certificate remains valid for up to two years. Before that period ends, the key must be renewed if it is still needed. If a certificate must be canceled (because a key was compromised or a person left the organization), the issuer publishes a Revoked Certificate List (RCL).

Each organization maintains an RCL signed with its private key, allowing recipients to verify the list came from the issuer. RCLs are published on a schedule announced by the issuer, and recipients are expected to cache and check them before accepting certificates.

For interoperation with other certification authorities (such as government or foreign systems), the RFC allows cross-certification: CAs can sign each other's certificates, creating bridges between separate hierarchies.
sections.plainLanguage: If Alice loses her key or leaves the company, they add her to a "revoked" list and sign it. Everyone checking certificates consults this list so they know not to trust her old key anymore.
